newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan won't derail derivatives rules - FASB.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan won't derail derivatives rules - FASB.

text.p: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) said Monday it plans to complete its controversial derivatives accounting rules, despite recent criticism from Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan, who urged the panel to slow down to allow more industry input.
The FASB also criticized Greenspan's suggested alternative for improving how companies report their derivatives holdings.
"Your approach -- when compared to ours -- would reduce the information available to investors and creditors," wrote FASB Chairman Edmund Jenkins in an Aug. 11 letter.
"We will carefully consider your comments and those of others as we move through the final stages of the process," Jenkins said.

The accounting board's latest correspondence follows Greenspan's request last week that FASB scrap its accounting proposals, which would require companies to report in their financial statements the flucuations in value of the derivatives they own.

Greenspan, siding with the concerns of the corporate community, called the FASB plan "a piecemeal approach" and warned the standards could drive companies from using derivatives to hedge against risk and could present misleading financial information.
As an alterntive, Greenspan suggested the board call for expanded disclosure of corporate derivatives holdings without dramatically changing current accounting practices.
"Existing practices of accounting for derivatives and hedging, which are similar to your suggested alternative, also are a piecmeal approach," the board countered.
Last month FASB opted move ahead with a final rule on the accounting for derivatives used in heding, even against the wishes of key market players and some top lawmakers.
The rules require that all derivatives be recognized in the financial statement. Gains and losses resulting from changes in fair values would be accounted for depending on the use of the derivative.
The accounting panel on Monday received needed support from a group of U.S. accountants.
The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants warned in a statement that investor protection, not politics, should guide financial reporting in this complex area.
